title: THE MACHINE
sub: How the federal government is wired: who does what, how they get the seat, and who can stop them.

layer1.title: Meet the branches
layer1.line: Four cards: the House, the Senate, the President and the Supreme Court. Same words as your chart.

rows.label: WHO
lines: House of Representatives
435 members*, seats split by each state's population

rows.label: HOW YOU GET THE SEAT
lines: At least 25 years old
A citizen for 7 years
Lives in the state
Elected by the voters in their district*
2-year term, no limit

rows.label: ITS POWERS
lines: Starts every tax bill
Impeaches: brings the charges

rows.label: WHO
lines: Senate
100 senators, 2 from every state

rows.label: HOW YOU GET THE SEAT
lines: At least 30 years old
A citizen for 9 years
Lives in the state
Elected by the voters of the whole state (since 1913, 17th Amendment)
6-year term, no limit

rows.label: ITS POWERS
lines: Holds the impeachment trial (two-thirds of the senators present to remove)
Approves treaties (two-thirds of the senators present)
Approves the President's picks for judges and top jobs

rows.label: BOTH HOUSES, TOGETHER
lines: Pass laws (both must agree) · tax and borrow · regulate trade · coin money · declare war · raise an army and navy · the Elastic Clause: make all laws "necessary and proper" to carry out these powers. It lets Congress use tools the Constitution never names, like a bank, to carry out the powers it does name.

rows.label: WHO CAN STOP IT
lines: The President can veto its bills
The Court can strike down its laws

rows.label: WHO
lines: The President
plus the Vice President

rows.label: HOW YOU GET THE SEAT
lines: At least 35 years old
A natural-born citizen
Lived in the U.S. 14 years
Chosen by the Electoral College: 270 of 538 votes wins*
4-year term, elected twice at most (22nd Amendment)

rows.label: ITS POWERS
lines: Carries out the laws
Commander in Chief of the military
Signs or vetoes bills
Makes treaties
Picks judges and top officials
Pardons federal crimes

rows.label: WHO CAN STOP IT
lines: Congress can override a veto (two-thirds of both houses)
The Senate can reject treaties and picks
The House impeaches; the Senate can remove
The Court can rule an action unconstitutional

rows.label: WHO
lines: 9 justices*: the Chief Justice and 8 others
plus the lower federal courts Congress creates

rows.label: HOW YOU GET THE SEAT
lines: No age or citizenship rule in the Constitution
Nominated by the President, approved by the Senate
Serves "during good Behaviour": for life, unless impeached and removed

rows.label: ITS POWERS
lines: Decides cases about the Constitution and federal law
Judicial Review: can strike down a law or action that breaks the Constitution

rows.label: WHO CAN STOP IT
lines: The President picks the justices
The Senate can reject them
Congress can impeach and remove judges
An amendment can overturn a ruling

foot: * Set by law, not by the Constitution's words.
Judicial Review isn't written in the Constitution. The Court claimed it in Marbury v. Madison (1803).

layer2.title: Final Say
layer2.line: Something happens. Tap the power that answers it.

items.situation: Congress passes a bill. The President hates it.
items.question: What can the President do?
items.why: The President sends it back unsigned, with the objections (Article I, Section 7).

items.situation: The President vetoed the bill. Congress still wants it.
items.question: What can Congress do back?
items.answer: Override the veto with two-thirds of both houses
wrong: Ask the Court to sign it
Pass it again by a simple majority
items.why: Two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate make it law anyway (Article I, Section 7).

items.situation: A law is challenged in court. The justices decide it breaks the Constitution.
items.question: What can the Court do?
items.why: That's Judicial Review. The Court claimed it in Marbury v. Madison (1803).

items.situation: A seat on the Supreme Court opens.
items.question: Who fills it?
items.answer: The President nominates; the Senate approves
items.why: "by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate" (Article II, Section 2).

items.situation: The President signs a treaty with another country.
items.question: What has to happen before it counts?
items.answer: Two-thirds of the senators present approve it
items.why: Treaties need two-thirds of the senators present (Article II, Section 2).

items.situation: A President is accused of bribery.
items.question: Who brings the charges, and who holds the trial?
items.answer: The House impeaches; the Senate holds the trial
wrong: The Senate charges; the House decides
items.why: Removal takes two-thirds of the senators present (Article I, Sections 2 and 3; Article II, Section 4).

items.situation: The country needs more money for the army.
items.question: Where does the tax bill have to start?
items.why: "All Bills for raising Revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives" (Article I, Section 7). The House is the part that faces the voters every two years.

items.situation: Another country attacks the United States.
items.question: Who can declare war? Who commands the troops?
items.answer: Congress declares war; the President commands
wrong: The Court declares war; Congress commands
items.why: Article I, Section 8 gives war to Congress; Article II, Section 2 makes the President Commander in Chief.

items.situation: A 32-year-old senator wants to run for President.
items.question: Can she?
items.answer: Not yet: a President must be at least 35
items.why: Article II, Section 1 sets the age at 35. Even a senator has to follow the rules.

items.situation: A popular President has been elected twice.
items.question: Can he run for a third term?
items.answer: No: the 22nd Amendment allows two elected terms
wrong: Yes, if the people want him
items.why: Ratified in 1951, after FDR won four times.

items.situation: Congress creates a national bank. The Constitution never mentions a bank.
items.question: How can Congress do it?
items.why: Article I, Section 8. In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Court upheld the bank and struck down Maryland's tax on it.

items.situation: Your state wants to raise the age for a driver's license.
items.question: Who decides?
items.answer: The state: it's a reserved power
items.why: The 10th Amendment keeps powers like this with the states.

layer2.done: You worked the machine. When it shows up in a unit, you'll know what you're looking at.
